implementation_notes: Ownership makes the classic pair impossible without a lock or an atomic: two `&mut` buffers cannot coexist, so the idiomatic double buffer is two `Arc<Frame>` snapshots and one published reference. `arc_swap::ArcSwap` - 'a container for an Arc that can be changed atomically' - provides `load()` (returning a guard that keeps the loaded frame alive), `store()` and `swap()`; it is the direct analogue of `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr>` from C++. Build the next frame in a locally owned value, publish it as a fresh `Arc`, and let the old one drop when the last guard goes away. When both buffers are owner-side scratch, plain `std::mem::swap` between two owned values is the whole pattern.
pitfalls: Holding a `load()` guard across long work delays reclamation of the previous frames; clone it if the frame must outlive the guard's scope.
Publishing an `Arc` whose contents are still mutated (`Arc<Mutex<..>>`, `Arc<RefCell<..>>` shared across threads) reintroduces the race the swap was meant to remove.
`Arc` is shared ownership, not a snapshot copy: readers must not assume the object they loaded is the one the writer is filling next.
Rust atomics follow the C++20 memory model; hand-rolled `AtomicPtr`/`AtomicUsize` publication moves the acquire/release reasoning and the unsafe reclamation onto you.

variants.name: std RwLock<Arc<T>> pair (std-only form)
variants.implementation_notes: A std-only alternative: hold the current frame in `RwLock<Arc<Frame>>`, build the next frame outside the lock, then take the write lock once and `std::mem::replace` the `Arc` - a single pointer swap under the lock - while readers take the read lock and clone the `Arc`, which keeps the old frame alive after the guard drops. No external crate and no unsafe code, at the cost of lock contention on a hot read path; it is the right form when the swap is rare and correctness matters more than the last nanoseconds.
pitfalls: `RwLock` is not reentrant and a panicking writer poisons it, making later `read()`/`write()` calls fail with `PoisonError`.
Writer starvation is possible with a steady stream of readers on some platforms; do not put the swap in a hot loop.
Holding the write lock while building the next frame serializes everything - build outside, swap inside.
Cloning the `Arc` out keeps the old frame alive; storing snapshots indefinitely delays reclamation even though the swap is O(1).
